Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
Fresh data points from September showed the housing market continues to deteriorate just as the Federal Reserve is considering raising interest rates again.
Building permits, new starts and pending sales all were considerably worse than Wall Street forecasts.
Under some circumstances, Fed officials would use easier policy to spur demand. However, the central bank is currently battling inflation, which it could prioritize over a flagging housing picture.
Workers install roofing for a new home under construction in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, June 29, 2026.
The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist.
Housing data deteriorated further in September , according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates.
Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage.
"The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze."
The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%.
Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday.
Pending home sales drop 7.3% in September, missing estimates
Privately owned housing starts fell 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data.
Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023.
"Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates."
The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily . Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices.
Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years.
Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs.
But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009.
Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing.
However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday.
"In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months."
Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall.
The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels. Walker attributed the middling levels as a product of the "lock-in" effect in which it's too expensive for current homeowners to move and take on higher borrowing costs while deteriorating affordability weighs on new construction.
"Housing activity has remained rangebound in recent years, capped on the upside by affordability headwinds and buffered on the downside by the longstanding housing shortage," Walker wrote. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity."
Markets expect the Fed to hold benchmark rates steady when it meets next week. However, futures pricing implies a strong chance of a quarter-point hike in December and another in March 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
One point of optimism comes from Yun, the NAR economist, who thinks the trend of mortgage costs running ahead of Fed hikes could mean that rates are topping out.
"Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve's short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out," he said. "Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably."

items.content:
Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there
By Stefanie Glinski ; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz Island
Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.
In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.
He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home
Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.
Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.
Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.
Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.
According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.
Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel .
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.
Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street
Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.
Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption
Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.
Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas
“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.
Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.
Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years
Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.
A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island
Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.
The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.
Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict
The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war
“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.
The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions
From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.
Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.
Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.
“Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”

Russia's President Vladimir Putin greets US special envoy Steve Witkoff prior to their meeting in Saint Petersburg on October 21, 2026 [Gavrill Grigorov/AFP]
Russian President Vladimir Putin has conveyed his “in principle” willingness to resume three-way talks to end the conflict in Ukraine to US special envoy Steve Witkoff, the Kremlin has said.
Witkoff held talks with Putin on Wednesday, as Washington pushes for an end to the Ukraine war that began more than four and a half years ago with Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Zelenskyy to hold talks on Russia-Ukraine war with Witkoff, Europeans
list 2 of 3 Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space?
list 3 of 3 ‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal
“Steve Witkoff briefed Vladimir Putin on the substance of the talks held in Oslo,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, referring to talks Witkoff held in Norway with Ukrainian and European officials on Tuesday.
“He mentioned some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv … but there wasn’t really much substance in them.”
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the mentioned talks [with Washington and Kyiv],” he added, saying they could take place in mid-November.
He later told Russian state television Vesti that the talks may be held in Abu Dhabi.
The last US-mediated peace ⁠talks took place in February before the United States and ⁠Israel launched a war against Iran.
The three-hour talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with ⁠a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia.
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia is obviously interested in the lifting of international sanctions, and US sanctions in particular.
“The Trump administration is using economic leverage to encourage Moscow to finish this war, including the temporary lifting of US sanctions on Russian diesel sales,” she said.
Putin also thanked US President Donald Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war.
Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, but Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to “make a deal”. He said on Tuesday it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face “a very bad thing”.
Putin also offered to help Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Moscow had a decades-long relationship with Tehran, which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the US to help farmers, Putin told Witkoff.
A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first meeting of its kind in history.
The talks in Russia come a day after Witkoff met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in Norway. Witkoff briefed Putin on the Oslo talks , which he described as productive and said had been characterised by “some degree of momentum”.
The prime ministers of Norway and Finland also attended the talks in Oslo. Representatives from the European Union and NATO were present. Following Tuesday’s talks, Zelenskyy said that “very, very important” intelligence from the US had been restored.
US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month.
Zelenskyy has also accused Washington of slowing down the internet service, Starshield , which is crucial for Ukraine’s battlefield operations. Starshield is the military-grade equivalent of Starlink – both developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk ordered the slowdown of the service, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.
Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv’s ability to access Starlink.
As diplomatic efforts intensify, Russia and Ukraine continue to trade long-range attacks.
At least one person was killed and two were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack in Russia’s western Bryansk region on Wednesday, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said on Telegram.
The Ukrainian emergency service said two people were killed in a Russian attack on a high-rise building in the Sviatoshinsky district of the capital, Kyiv.

(Kitco NewsWire) – Spot  gold prices were slightly higher and spot  silver prices were lower in early U.S. trading Wednesday, as renewed concerns about energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz and persistent expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening weighed on precious metals. Gold found some support from lower Treasury yields and defensive demand, while silver struggled to sustain Tuesday's recovery amid uncertainty surrounding industrial activity and the interest rate outlook. At the time of the latest verified morning price reading, spot gold was trading near $4,136.70 an ounce, up $12.60, or 0.31%, while spot silver was trading near $57.510, down $0.370, or 0.64%.
Market positioning remains divided between signs of weakening economic activity and stubborn inflation pressure. September consumer prices increased 0.6% on the month and 3.7% annually, while producer prices surged 1.3% and 6.3%, respectively. Despite those inflation surprises, traders continue to assign approximately an 83% probability that the Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting. Expectations for another rate increase remain concentrated in December, with futures indicating roughly a 94% probability that rates will be higher by the Dec. 9 meeting. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was trading near the 5.1% area Wednesday morning, down from recent highs above 5.3%, as weaker housing activity and concerns about financial-market stability supported government bonds. The dollar's broader resilience and the prospect of additional Fed tightening continue to limit gold's upside potential despite some relief from lower yields.
The Federal Reserve remains in its premeeting communications blackout, leaving incoming economic releases and energy-market developments as the principal drivers of interest rate expectations. Wednesday's calendar includes the weekly U.S. petroleum inventory report at 10:30 a.m. EDT and a 20-year Treasury bond auction at 1 p.m. EDT. Thursday brings weekly initial jobless claims at 8:30 a.m. EDT, followed Friday by preliminary October manufacturing and services purchasing managers' indexes at 9:45 a.m. EDT and the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading at 10 a.m. EDT. Softer employment and business activity figures could reinforce concerns about slowing growth and reduce December tightening expectations, supporting gold through lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar. However, persistently elevated inflation expectations or renewed energy-price increases would strengthen the case for additional Fed tightening and maintain pressure on non-yielding bullion.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remains a significant source of volatility in global energy and precious metals markets. Oil prices rebounded Wednesday following reports of additional attacks on commercial shipping in the strategic waterway, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi signaled that prospects for a near-term peace agreement with Washington remain limited. The latest escalation followed Tuesday's sharp intraday reversal in crude prices amid conflicting reports about potential diplomatic negotiations. The underlying supply situation remains fragile despite a recovery in overall Middle Eastern crude exports. Regional oil shipments averaged approximately 24.6 million barrels per day in the week ending Oct. 18, exceeding the prewar average of 23.3 million barrels per day as producers expanded alternative export routes. However, shipments directly through Hormuz remained approximately 33% below prewar levels, while attacks on vessels and infrastructure continued to threaten the reliability of regional energy supplies. Brent crude climbed back above $110.00 a barrel Wednesday, reinforcing concerns about the inflationary consequences of a prolonged regional conflict.
For gold, continued uncertainty surrounding Gulf security supports defensive demand, but higher crude prices also reinforce inflation expectations and the prospect of restrictive U.S. monetary policy. This competing influence helps explain why bullion has struggled to sustain rallies despite the continuing geopolitical conflict. Silver faces similar interest rate headwinds, with its industrial exposure adding sensitivity to signs of weaker economic activity. The prospect of further Fed tightening, alongside uncertainty about the direction of oil prices, continues to complicate the near-term outlook for both metals.
Global equity markets were mixed to firmer before the U.S. open, with technology shares recovering amid a fresh round of corporate earnings. Nasdaq futures advanced approximately 0.4% and S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%, while Dow futures were little changed. Asian markets were generally firmer, with South Korea's Kospi gaining approximately 3.3% and Japan's Nikkei 225 advancing as investors returned to semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related shares. European markets were mixed, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 near unchanged, Germany's DAX slightly lower and France's CAC 40 posting modest gains. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 weakened amid pressure on mining shares. Investors are also assessing quarterly corporate results and the implications of elevated financing costs for technology-sector investment, while continuing fiscal uncertainty in France has kept European government bond markets under pressure.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil prices higher and trading near $99.40 a barrel, while Brent crude was near $111.00. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note is trading near the 5.1% area. The U.S. dollar index is slightly firmer in early dealings, continuing to reflect expectations that U.S. monetary policy will remain restrictive despite recent evidence of slowing economic activity. ( Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)

Gold Declines Towards $4,120 as Iran Conflict and Federal Reserve Outlook Remain in Focus
Gold coin ©PIX1861 Gold prices declined on Wednesday as investors assessed uncertainty surrounding efforts to end the conflict between the United States and Iran, alongside expectations for US interest rates and the potential inflationary effects of higher energy costs.
At 02:36 ET (06:36 GMT), spot gold was down 0.2% at $4,117.31 per ounce, while US gold futures fell 0.2% to $4,134.92 per ounce.
Other precious metals also traded lower. Silver declined 1.2% to $57.2955 per ounce, platinum lost 1.8% to $1,627.45, and spot palladium decreased 1.6% to $1,088.40.
The US Dollar Index edged up 0.1% to 101.80, adding to the market conditions affecting dollar-denominated commodities.
Gold has fallen more than 1% since the beginning of the week and remains approximately 20% below its level when the US-Iran conflict began in late February.
The conflict has disrupted energy supplies and contributed to higher oil prices, complicating the inflation outlook and expectations for monetary policy.
Higher interest rates can affect demand for gold because the metal does not generate interest income, making interest-bearing assets comparatively more attractive.
Oil Price Movements Reflect Uncertainty Over Iran Negotiations
Oil prices stabilised on Wednesday after retreating from a five-month high during the previous session.
The decline followed reports suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to an agreement to end the conflict. However, a diplomat subsequently dismissed suggestions that a settlement was imminent.
Gold prices initially increased as oil declined following the reports of possible negotiations, before reversing those gains when energy prices recovered.
The US dollar and government bond yields also moved lower during the period of fluctuating oil prices.
Market participants continued to assess the potential implications of the conflict for global energy supplies, inflation and economic activity.
The relationship between energy prices and inflation expectations remains particularly relevant to gold, given the influence of monetary policy expectations on demand for non-interest-bearing assets.
US Treasury securities with longer maturities gained as oil prices retreated and economic data indicated softer conditions in parts of the US economy.
September housing starts declined, while pending home sales fell to a record low, providing further evidence of reduced activity in the housing market.
The figures added to the economic information being considered ahead of the Federal Reserve's next monetary policy meeting, scheduled for 27–28 October.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's comments on Friday did not materially change market expectations for the upcoming decision.
Investors continued to anticipate that the central bank would leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at the October meeting.
Market pricing indicated a probability of less than 17% that the Fed would increase rates by 25 basis points at that meeting.
However, inflation remains above the central bank's 2% target, and traders were assigning approximately an 85% probability to another interest rate increase before the end of the year.
Warsh's remarks came ahead of the Federal Reserve's communications blackout period, which begins on Saturday and restricts public commentary from policymakers before the meeting.
With limited additional guidance expected from central bank officials, investors are monitoring economic indicators, Treasury yields and developments in the Middle East for information that could influence interest rate expectations.
Gold and other precious metals remained under pressure during Wednesday's trading as markets continued to evaluate the interaction between energy prices, inflation and the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

items.title: The Stock Market is Flashing Several Warning Signs at Once. Does That Mean a Crash is Imminent? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Stock Market is Flashing Several Warning Signs at Once. Does That Mean a Crash is Imminent?  The Motley
items.content:
There have been many headlines recently about the stock market flashing warning signs. I've even written some of them . However, even when several signs flash at once, they don't mean a crash is imminent because they don't all tell us the same thing.
Instead, what they do signal is that now is the time to be more prepared. Here's how to read these signs and prepare your portfolio for what could lie ahead.
The stock market regularly experiences meaningful downdrafts. It has historically corrected (a 10% or more decline) roughly once every 18 months and tumbled into a bear market (a 20% or more drop) about once every six years. However, it doesn't move in that exact pattern. That's why investors are always looking for signs that another meaningful decline could be on the horizon.
One sign that has historically preceded a major decline is an elevated CAPE ratio (cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio). It measures whether the market is undervalued or overvalued relative to its historical inflation-adjusted earnings record. It's currently at 40.5; it's the second-highest reading in 150 years. Its prior peak was just before the dot-com crash. It was last above 40 in late 2021, right before the 2022 rate-driven bear market.
Speaking of rates, the Federal Reserve just started raising interest rates for the first time in three years. According to data from LPL Financial , the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.51% ) has declined in five of the last six Fed rate-hike cycles (including 2022).
Finally, there's margin debt, which has surged 49% over the past year. According to data from Fundstrat Global Advisors, the market has declined five out of six times when margin debt has surged 45% or more year-over-year since 1960.
While all that sounds foreboding, none of these signs mean a crash is forthcoming, as they're not perfect predictors. For example, while a high CAPE ratio is a strong indicator of lower market returns over the longer term, it doesn't mean the market will crash next year. For example, it was above 30 in 2018. The next year, the S&P 500 rose 29%. It's also worth noting that the S&P 500 didn't decline during the 1997 rate-hike cycle (though that was only a 25-basis-point increase). Meanwhile, the S&P 500 was up 12 months following a 45% (or more) year-over-year increase in margin debt one out of every six times. For example, it last hit that level in October 2025, but was up 10.9% 12 months later.
So, we shouldn't read all these signs as imminent warnings of a crash. Instead, they should serve more as a reminder that the market does correct from time to time, and we need to ensure our portfolios remain prepared for the next downturn.
One way we can do that is by selling lower-conviction holdings to raise cash and by trimming positions where current valuations require perfect execution to deliver acceptable returns. That would build cash to capitalize on a meaningful decline in the coming months.
Now's also the time to build a watch list of stocks you want to buy if there is a downdraft. For example, Alphabet ( GOOG -2.29% ) ( GOOGL -2.21% ) is one of my higher-conviction holdings. It has a dominant search business and a growing cloud business, which is just scratching the surface of its AI potential. However, at 26 times forward earnings, Alphabet isn't cheap enough for me to add to right now, given that the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index trades at about 21.5 times forward earnings. It's also investing heavily in AI ($180 billion to $190 billion this year), increasing its risks. While Alphabet's AI investments could drive meaningful growth in the coming years, I'd like a little more margin of safety. If Alphabet's stock got down closer to $300 per share (around 22.5x forward earnings), I'd start buying more.

With the market flashing lots of warning signs these days, it's easy to become fearful that it's about to crash. However, there's no guarantee this will happen, as these aren't perfect predictors. Meanwhile, even if a downdraft did happen, it's far better to see one not as a threat but as an opportunity. The best way to do that is to use the warning signs as a signal to be better prepared by building cash and a watch list now, so you can capitalize on any potential opportunities that may arise in the near term.

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Smartest Move Investors Can Make - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Smartest Move Investors Can Make  The Motley Fool
items.content:
After a year of record-breaking gains, major market indexes are wobbling. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.51% ) has fallen by nearly 2% over the last week, as of this writing, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +1.09% ) is down by more than 4% in that time.
Much of the sell-off is stemming from the tech sector, with artificial intelligence (AI) spending under the microscope. Rising bond yields have driven up borrowing costs, making it more expensive for AI hyperscalers to continue building data centers and related infrastructure. If big tech companies pull back on AI spending, it could cause a ripple effect across the broader market.
At this point, it's too soon to tell whether this volatility is a blip on the radar or the beginning of a deeper drawdown. Regardless of what's coming, though, Warren Buffett has one tried-and-tested strategy that can set your portfolio up for success.
In a 1999 essay for Fortune , Warren Buffett issued a warning to investors. The stock market was reaping the rewards of the dot-com boom, with the S&P 500 surging by nearly 200% over the previous four years, but Buffett predicted stock prices would fall.
He also emphasized that when an industry is poised to transform society, it's especially important to choose your investments carefully. Buffett mentioned airlines as an example, noting that while air travel itself has had a monumental impact on our lives, 129 airlines had filed for bankruptcy over the previous 20 years.
Buffett's 1999 warning eventually rang true, as the dot-com bubble officially popped in early 2000 -- leading to a bear market that would last more than two years. Hundreds of tech stocks crashed and burned, despite the internet's revolutionary impact on the world.
"The key to investing is not assessing how much an industry is going to affect society, or how much it will grow," Buffett said in the Fortune essay, "but rather determining the competitive advantage of any given company and, above all, the durability of that advantage."
When the dot-com bubble burst, overvalued stocks crashed the hardest. These companies earned explosive returns when the bubble was building, but many had unsustainable business models, poorly managed finances, or inexperienced leadership teams that couldn't navigate the bear market.
Now, we could be facing a similar situation. AI, as a technology, could transform the world. But not every company in the AI space will thrive. Many tech stocks have seen eye-popping returns this year, but it's likely that at least a few of them have been driven by hype and are overvalued right now.
This doesn't mean that all stocks will struggle over time, though. Since the start of the dot-com bear market in March 2000, for example, the S&P 500 has soared by more than 715%. While many companies failed, some tech stocks of the era -- like Apple , Amazon , and Microsoft -- went on to become industry-leading giants.
Overvalued stocks from weak companies will be hit the hardest whenever the next bear market arrives. Companies with strong fundamentals and a durable competitive advantage, however, have the best chance at recovering and going on to earn positive long-term returns.
The single best move investors can make right now is to load up on quality stocks. The healthier your portfolio, the more likely it is to survive even a severe downturn. In Buffett's words: "The products or services that have wide, sustainable moats around them are the ones that deliver rewards to investors."

items.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
items.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
items.content:
By Rachel Clun Business reporter ,Â  Reporting from New York
US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.
The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.
The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.
The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.
Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.
The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.
That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".
The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.
It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.
Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.
"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.
The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.
"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.
The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.
It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.
Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

items.title: Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict?
items.summary: The European states say their support for Riyadh is 'defensive', but analysts warn Houthi reaction may complicate that.
items.content:
Share Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict? on social media
Typhoon fighter jets operate from a British air station in Coningsby, UK, October 21 [Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images]
France and the United Kingdom have both moved to deploy military assets to Saudi Arabia, deepening their defence ties with the kingdom as its conflict with the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), in Yemen escalates.
Paris last week said it had begun sending assets to Saudi Arabia as part of a previously announced agreement, after President Emmanuel Macron committed to deploying troops and air defence systems to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis .

list 2 of 2 UK to deploy Typhoon jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
The UK , for its part, on Tuesday announced plans to deploy fighter jets to help shield Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks.
Both countries stressed that their support would be defensive.
Analysts say the European moves serve several geopolitical purposes: protecting Saudi oil exports that are important to European energy markets, shoring up their strategic alliance in the Gulf amid US reluctance to offer direct military assistance to Saudi Arabia, and strengthening deterrence against future Houthi attacks.
But the deployments also carry significant risks, many analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states more directly into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.
“If insufficiently deterred, the Houthis may decide that the moment is ripe to test the resolve and resilience of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture, and attempt to draw Saudi Arabia’s allies even further into the Yemen-Saudi confrontation,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East Security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera.
The British and French military support measures come as Saudi Arabia faces a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign against it , including targeting energy and transport infrastructure.
Houthi attacks targeting Saudi airports in Riyadh and Abha this month have killed 19 people and injured more than 300 others, according to the Saudi-led coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki.
Addressing the UK’s stepped-up military support for Saudi Arabia, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia “absolutely despicable”, specifically condemning the group’s targeting of Riyadh airport.
The UK Ministry of Defence said it would deploy Typhoon fighter jets to fly “defensive counter air missions” in Saudi Arabia, send UK military advisers to work with Saudi staff officers and provide an A400M transport aircraft to help move defence material within the kingdom.
French support for Saudi Arabia would include soldiers, radars and defence systems, Macron has said, without detailing the scale of the support.
Urban Coningham, a research fellow at RUSI, noted differences in the British and French roles, with the French mainly limited to protecting Saudi export infrastructure. The British, by contrast, will conduct “defensive patrols where they would shoot down incoming missiles or drones” in Saudi Arabia, as well as provide air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi bombers and jets heading into Yemeni airspace, he said.
Camille Lons, policy fellow and deputy head of the Paris office at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France is limited in what it can provide to Saudi Arabia, particularly given the demands on European defences amid the war in Ukraine. Still, Paris sees its assistance as a way to “show support [for Saudi Arabia] in times of crisis, and a way to deepen the defence partnership”, Lons told Al Jazeera.
Saudi Arabia will welcome the European deployments, as it has struggled to translate some of its security partnerships into high-level military support.
In September, US President Donald Trump rejected multiple Saudi requests to participate in strikes on the Houthis, agreeing only to provide intelligence and targeting support, the news agency Reuters cited informed sources saying.
Turkiye and Pakistan have committed to “collective deterrence measures”, including potential troop deployments, under the newly signed Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia, but the agreement has yet to be ratified in Turkiye .
Egypt’s parliament has also postponed a vote that would authorise its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia.
Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at King’s College War Studies Department, called the UK and French deployments “militarily valuable and politically significant”, saying they could help shield the kingdom’s sprawling territory from persistent Houthi air attacks while giving Riyadh more room to focus its own assets on offensive operations.
“The British Typhoons can reinforce Saudi air defences and, crucially, free up Saudi Eurofighters for offensive operations,” Obaid told Al Jazeera. “France’s contribution is particularly important for protecting Yanbu.”
Saudi Arabia “does not need foreign assistance to conduct air strikes”, Obaid added, noting that the kingdom has its own powerful combat aircraft fleet. “What it needs is additional defensive coverage across its enormous territory, particularly for critical energy infrastructure.”
Ozcelik said the recent British move was “not insignificant”, but its deterrent impact was not immediately clear.
“The question remains whether the UK air missions will move the dial in deterring sustained Houthi attacks while Saudi air defences and interceptor stockpiles are stretched,” said Ozcelik. “The difference between deterrence and interdiction is an important one.”
What also remains to be seen is whether the UK and France will maintain a purely defensive posture – and whether the Houthis will recognise that distinction at all.
Coningham said the Houthis could interpret European military involvement, especially the UK’s air-to-air support for Saudi bombers and jets, as “offensive” rather than defensive, leading the group to view those countries as belligerents and their forces as targets.
As a result, Coningham said, the Houthis could strike at British forces stationed in the region – whether in Saudi Arabia or elsewhere, such as Cyprus – or reverse their position on allowing free transit to non-Saudi vessels, including European ships, in the Bab al-Mandeb strait – a key maritime route in the world.
Another potential flashpoint would be a Houthi attack in Saudi Arabia that kills British or French personnel, analysts noted.
“Whether it’s a direct attack planned by the Houthis or collateral damage, if the British or French have any casualties … then there becomes a pointed debate in those countries as to whether they should then retaliate,” said Coningham.
Ozcelik said the UK could face pressure to play a more offensive role in the event of a “mass civilian casualty event” caused by the Houthis or “debilitating attacks on Saudi’s energy infrastructure”, although London would likely view such a scenario as a “last resort”.
“Neither the Mecca signatories nor the UK are inclined to get dragged into deeper and likely protracted conflict inside Yemen,” said Ozcelik.

items.title: Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin - CBS News
items.summary: Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin  CBS News
items.content:
Progress toward a negotiated resolution to Russia's war on Ukraine is "theoretically possible," Kremlin officials said Wednesday as U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, but any headway will require Ukraine's leaders to make "necessary decisions," according to Russian state media.
If Ukraine fails to make those decisions, the situation for the country "will be worse," the officials said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.
During Witkoff's meeting with Putin, he and the Russian leader confirmed that Stephen Hubbard , a U.S. citizen jailed in Russia for more than four years, had been released from custody. President Trump said Putin agreed to free the American with "no 'swap' necessary," but he also said it wouldn't have happened had the U.S. not prevented new sanctions against Moscow from taking effect last week. Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing Hubbard, sparking backlash in the U.S.
State media said Russian officials told Witkoff on Wednesday that a meeting between Mr. Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping was "possible," referring to an idea the White House has also floated, but Ukrainian officials have balked at as it would sideline them from talks on their own country's fate.
Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026.
Video of the meeting as it opened Wednesday showed Witkoff saying he hoped to discuss the resumption of trilateral talks between Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine. The Kremlin did not initially indicate any new willingness to engage, and Russian officials said before the gathering in St. Petersburg that Moscow's position and demands had not changed.
After the meeting, Putin's senior foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov was quoted by TASS as saying the Russian leader told Witkoff that Moscow was "generally ready" to resume trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine in early November, and that the two men had "specifically discussed a potential framework for resuming trilateral negotiations."
But Ushakov also said, according to a Kremlin transcript of his remarks, that the proposals brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, which he attributed to Ukraine and the European Union, "contained little that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that he believed trilateral talks between himself, Mr. Trump and Putin were the best way to resolve the conflict, and that he would not accept any resolution crafted by China, Russia and the U.S., saying: "Don't talk about us without us."
Zelenskyy also said any negotiated end to the war would need to be approved by Ukraine's Parliament.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told journalists on a separate trip Wednesday that Witkoff held "positive" talks with Zelenskyy on Tuesday in Oslo before traveling to Russia, and that he would share ideas discussed with Zelenskyy with the Russian side in an attempt to "make some progress."
After that meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Zelenskyy thanked Washington for restoring U.S. intelligence sharing on Russian strikes, after saying this week that his country had stopped receiving advance warnings of imminent Russian missile strikes.
"We are thankful that intelligence works," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo. He said the early warnings for ballistic missiles were "very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians."
Zelenskyy told Fox on Wednesday, however, that access to data from the Starshield satellite network, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink system, remained "limited" in Ukraine , but that Rubio was working on it and expected full access to be restored.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, right, and Masud Gharahkhani, the president of Norway's Parliament, speak to journalists on Oct. 21, 2026, in Oslo.
Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations with European officials following his visit to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he said "a lot depends on whether the American side manages to hear something new from Russia today."
The diplomacy comes after weeks of friction between Kyiv and Washington, with Mr. Trump criticizing Zelenskyy for Ukraine's continued response to relentless, deadly Russian strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Mr. Trump announced an " energy ceasefire " earlier in the month, claiming both sides had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, but within hours Russia launched new missile attacks on Ukrainian refineries and other sites, and neither Ukraine nor Russia ever confirmed agreeing to a truce of any kind.
The U.S. president also announced a deal with Moscow on Oct. 10 for Russia to release millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months, which Zelenskyy labeled a sign of "weakness."
Russian state media said the first shipment of diesel had been dispatched for the U.S. on Wednesday.

Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix's momentum may be slowing. The company's forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts' expectations.
AT&T fell 4.9% even though it also delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts' expectations.
Among AI stocks, which have been at the center of the market's action in recent weeks, the movements were relatively steady, at least for now.
After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centers may slow because of how much more expensive it's become to borrow money.
CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky. On Oct. 20, it careened between a loss of 6% and a gain of 5%, for example. On Oct. 21, it added 0.1%.
Besides SpaceX's profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of "increased demand for AI platforms," and its stock rallied 13.2%.
PCS Software CEO Mark Hill discusses the advance of AI in the trucking industry. Tune in above or by going to RoadSigns.ttnews.com .
Another potential boost for the AI industry came from an easing of Treasury yields in the bond market, which helps dictate how expensive loans are for the U.S. government, companies and regular Americans.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.09% from 5.12% late Oct. 20, though it remains far above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation higher.
In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea's Kospi jumped 3.3% for one of the world's biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength.

Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 2026.
Oil prices were little changed Wednesday as worries over Middle East supply disruptions keep the market on edge, with attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy facilities denting sentiment.
Brent crude futures lost 17 cents to $108.62 a barrel as of 8:47 a.m. ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 8 cents to $97.90 a barrel.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that naval mines had prevented three tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz using routes Tehran deemed unauthorized.
"Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," IRGC said in a statement published on their official Sepah News website .
Adding to regional worries, Yemen's Houthi militants claimed responsibility on Monday for strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Riyadh and Abha.
The escalating tensions have also sent global oil shipping costs soaring, adding another layer of pressure to energy markets.
The global average crude freight rate has surged above $20 per barrel, compared with just $3 a year earlier, according to a Goldman Sachs report published Tuesday. While rates have eased slightly in recent days, they remain roughly seven times higher than a year ago.
Goldman estimated that war-risk premiums associated with crossing the Strait of Hormuz accounted for about $7 of the $20 year-on-year increase in average crude freight rates, while ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf contributed another $4.
The investment bank warned that elevated shipping costs could widen price differences between crude grades, squeeze refiners' profit margins and ultimately push up refined fuel prices.
"High freight costs have weighed particularly heavily on Asian refineries' net margins, threatening their refined product output, which could then raise global refined product prices," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote.

items.content:
US Stock Futures Edge Higher as SpaceX and Tesla Explore Merger and Meta Earnings Approach: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street NYSE stock exchange ©Shutterstock US stock futures traded mostly higher on Wednesday as investors assessed corporate earnings, developments in artificial intelligence investment and geopolitical uncertainty surrounding the conflict in the Middle East. Attention also turned to comments from Elon Musk about a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, reports concerning Anthropic's financial performance and Meta Platforms' forthcoming quarterly results.
US futures rise as investors assess earnings and oil prices
At 03:01 ET (07:01 GMT), S&P 500 futures were up 13 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq 100 futures gained 148 points, or 0.5%. Dow Jones futures were broadly unchanged.
Wall Street ended Tuesday's session with mixed results. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced, while the Nasdaq Composite closed slightly lower.
Oil prices fluctuated during the session following unconfirmed reports that Qatar and Pakistan had proposed renewed negotiations aimed at ending the conflict involving Iran. Brent crude briefly declined from approximately $112 to $106 per barrel before recovering.
The initial decline in energy prices coincided with gains in equities, which have recently been affected by concerns over borrowing costs and the scale of debt-financed investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
"The relief from energy that played out late in the European session meant equities rallied as investors overcame some of their earlier AI jitters," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a research note.
Brent subsequently returned to approximately $110 per barrel after reports of comments attributed to Iran's president concerning the possibility of further US military action.
Technology shares underperformed parts of the broader market. An index tracking semiconductor companies declined 0.29%, although it recovered much of its earlier losses. AI cloud infrastructure provider CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) also rebounded during the session.
SpaceX and Tesla establish committees to examine possible merger
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) have formed committees to evaluate a potential combination of the two businesses, according to Elon Musk, who serves as chief executive of both companies.
Speaking to investors following SpaceX's quarterly earnings announcement, Musk said the committees had not reached an agreement on "the terms of any transaction."
Musk, who is not a member of either committee, said there was "no guarantee" that a merger would take place, although he considered there to be "a lot of merit" in combining the businesses.
Shares in both companies advanced in after-hours trading following the comments.
A potential transaction would bring together SpaceX's rocket launch and satellite operations with Tesla's electric vehicle and related technology businesses. No transaction terms or timetable have been announced.
SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, an increase of more than 160% compared with the previous year and above analysts' expectations.
The company recorded profit of $4.4 billion, while capital expenditure reached $19.6 billion during the period.
The results marked SpaceX's second quarterly earnings publication since its initial public offering earlier in 2026.
Tesla is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results after Wednesday's market close.
Anthropic reports revenue growth alongside financial and operational risks
Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANTP) reported substantial revenue growth during the first half of the year, according to media reports citing disclosures associated with its potential initial public offering.
The company, which develops the Claude AI models, generated revenue of $16.3 billion during the six-month period.
Approximately 20% of that revenue came from two customers, highlighting the concentration of sales among a relatively small number of clients.
Anthropic indicated that a significant proportion of its revenue is expected to remain dependent on a limited customer base for the foreseeable future.
The company also identified uncertainty surrounding access to the computing infrastructure required to develop and operate its AI models.
Anthropic recorded a net loss exceeding $80 billion, compared with a loss of $13 billion in the corresponding period last year. The reported increase was largely attributed to an accounting adjustment.
Additional risks identified in the disclosures included potential legal liabilities arising from the use of artificial intelligence, including cybersecurity-related incidents.
Reports suggested that a future stock market listing could value Anthropic at approximately $2 trillion, although no confirmed IPO valuation was provided.
Meta earnings to provide update on AI investment plans
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is scheduled to release its quarterly earnings after Wednesday's closing bell, with investors focusing on revenue performance and the company's spending plans for artificial intelligence.
The owner of Facebook and Instagram has recently expanded its AI product portfolio following the September introduction of its Muse model.
According to the reported information, the product attracted millions of downloads following its launch, with applications including travel booking assistance and tools for small businesses.
Meta subsequently introduced an open-weight version of its Muse Spark model for coding applications.
The earnings announcement will provide an update on Meta's investment requirements as it expands its AI infrastructure and related services.
Large technology companies have committed substantial capital to advanced semiconductor purchases, computing capacity and data centre construction as they develop AI products.
Investors have increasingly focused on the relationship between these expenditures, financing requirements and the revenue generated by AI-related services.
Meta's results will therefore be examined for information on capital expenditure expectations and the financial contribution of its AI initiatives.
Nvidia reportedly considers additional investment in Firmus Grid
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is in discussions about investing hundreds of millions of dollars in Australian AI cloud infrastructure company Firmus Grid, according to a report by The Information.
Nvidia already holds an investment stake in Firmus and has invested in several other companies operating in the AI cloud infrastructure sector.
The reported discussions follow Firmus Grid's decision to abandon plans for an initial public offering in Australia earlier this month.
The company cited recent financial market volatility as a reason for withdrawing the proposed listing, which it said would not have been in shareholders' interests under the prevailing conditions.
Firmus had previously outlined plans for an IPO at a valuation exceeding $30 billion, potentially making it one of Australia's largest stock market listings.
The size, structure and timing of any additional Nvidia investment have not been confirmed.
US equity markets entered Wednesday's session with attention divided between corporate earnings, AI infrastructure financing and developments in the Middle East. The forthcoming results from Meta and Tesla, together with reported activity involving SpaceX, Anthropic and Nvidia, are among the company-specific developments being assessed by investors.

Wall Street Futures Rise as Corporate Earnings Support Technology Stocks: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq
Nasdaq sign on a tall building ©Dries Buytaert US stock index futures pointed to a higher opening on Wednesday, suggesting Wall Street could extend its gains from recent sessions as investors assessed quarterly earnings reports and prepared for further results from major technology companies.
Technology stocks were expected to contribute to the early advance, although individual companies recorded contrasting pre-market movements following their latest financial announcements.
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) shares rose 8.8% in pre-market trading after the rocket and space technology company led by Elon Musk reported third-quarter earnings above market expectations, supported by a substantial increase in revenue.
Musk also confirmed that SpaceX and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) had established independent special committees to examine a potential merger. No final decision regarding a transaction was announced.
Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) advanced 12.2% before the opening bell after the data centre server manufacturer raised its revenue outlook for the first quarter of its fiscal year.
In contrast, Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) declined 6.8% in pre-market trading. The streaming company reported third-quarter earnings that exceeded analysts' estimates but issued revenue guidance below market expectations.
AT&T (NYSE:T) shares also fell, losing 5% despite the telecommunications company reporting third-quarter revenue and earnings above forecasts.
Investors were also awaiting quarterly results from Tesla, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and IBM (NYSE:IBM), all scheduled for release after Wednesday's market close.
The anticipated higher opening followed a mixed performance on Wall Street on Tuesday, when stocks recovered from an initial decline before giving back part of their gains later in the session.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 529.85 points, or 1%, to close at 52,495.88, its highest closing level in more than a month. The S&P 500 gained 21.84 points, or 0.3%, to 7,712.57, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped 6.07 points, or less than 0.1%, to 26,424.82.
Industrial conglomerate 3M (NYSE:MMM) contributed to the Dow's advance, with its shares rising 6% after the company reported third-quarter earnings above expectations and increased its full-year profit forecast.
Other Dow constituents, including Amgen (NASDAQ:AMGN), Merck (NYSE:MRK) and UnitedHealth (NYSE:UNH), also recorded gains.
Movements in energy prices influenced trading sentiment during Tuesday's session. US crude oil futures fell substantially after earlier increases, following a report suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to a reduction in tensions between the United States and Iran.
According to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, negotiators from Qatar and Pakistan had presented a compromise proposal aimed at ending the conflict. The report cited a source suggesting that an announcement concerning a possible halt to the escalation could come during the week.
Neither the United States nor Iran had confirmed the reported proposal.
The decline in crude oil prices coincided with increased buying interest in equities, although investors remained attentive to geopolitical developments and forthcoming corporate earnings.
Among individual sectors, pharmaceutical stocks advanced, lifting the NYSE Arca Pharmaceutical Index by 2.8% to its highest closing level in two months.
Housing-related shares also gained, with the Philadelphia Housing Sector Index rising 2.6%.
Biotechnology, healthcare and airline stocks recorded increases alongside most other major market sectors.
Wednesday's session is expected to remain focused on corporate earnings, particularly the forthcoming announcements from Tesla, Meta Platforms and IBM, while developments in energy markets and US-Iran relations could also influence investor sentiment.

A 2027 turning point? Goldman, Citi see stabilising signs in China’s housing market
Encouraging holiday sales and shrinking supply point to recovery for country’s property sector, according to Goldman Sachs and Citi
As China’s housing market downturn enters its fifth year, global investment banks including Goldman Sachs and Citi say they expect the sector to pivot as soon as 2027, with expectations fuelled by signs of shrinking supply and robust sales over the National Day holiday in early October.
Citi holds a positive view on the sector and saw 2027 as a pivotal year for home price recovery in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. Home prices in China hit their lowest point in June 2024, according to Citi.
Shanghai became the first city to post positive year-on-year growth in secondary home prices in September, with prices rising 0.8 per cent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday.
“While we need further confirmation before declaring a sustained recovery, the evidence increasingly points to stabilising and potentially rising home prices in top cities, with most tier-two cities likely to lag,” said Griffin Chan, an analyst at Citi Research, in a report on Tuesday.
