I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Ukraine and ⁠US negotiators discussed the situation in ⁠the Russian-occupied ⁠town ​of Oleshky, Davyd Arakhamia – a member ⁠of Kyiv’s negotiating team – was quoted by ⁠local media via Reuters as ​saying.
“We ‌discussed it ‌yesterday, and the ‌informal outcome of this meeting is that there should be some good news ‌next week,” he told media outlet RBC-Ukraine.
Residents ​of the Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February ⁠2022, have reported a ​deepening ​food crisis ​as roads in and ​out ‌are ​heavily ​mined and saturated by drones.
‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Last week, Pope Leo urged Russia’s Vladimir Putin to allow humanitarian aid to the city.
We are still getting more lines from the Kremlin, with Interfax news agency reporting that a new round of trilateral Russia, US, Ukraine talks could take place in Abu Dhabi in mid-November.
Curiously, despite his less enthusiastic comments earlier, Interfax also has Kremlin’s Ushakov saying that “the Ukrainian conflict is heading toward its conclusion.”
There is also a fascinating story unfolding online, as government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely ⁠used programming language sent website operators scrambling ⁠to protect their systems, Reuters reported.
The Dutch National Cyber Security Center website is temporarily unavailable. Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock Developers of the ​PHP programming language said Tuesday they had identified two critical vulnerabilities and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix was released. They said on Wednesday that a new version fixing the vulnerabilities was live.
But with reports that hackers were ⁠exploiting the flaws to break into websites, government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline ahead of the fix as a precaution.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet, raising concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack.
Meanwhile, we now have a longer reaction from the Kremlin to the proposals US peace envoy Steve Witkoff relayed to president Vladimir Putin , warning they were “lacking substance.”
Russian president Vladimir Putin welcomes US president’s special envoy Steve Witkoff before a meeting in St. Petersburg, Russia. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL/EPA “Steve Witkoff briefed Vladimir Putin on the substance of the talks held in Oslo,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, referring to talks Witkoff held in Norway with Ukrainian and European officials on Tuesday.
“He mentioned some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv... but there wasn’t really much substance in them .”
(That’s very much not what Zelenskyy and the Europeans said last night. )
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the mentioned (trilateral) talks, ” he added, saying they could take place in mid-November.
Back again to Greece where tens of thousands of students have joined the burgeoning youth movement demanding better education better prospects amid an ever worsening cost of living crisis in the Mediterranean EU member.
Students, school pupils, teachers and university professors take part in a large education protest in Athens, Greece. Photograph: Harris Xanthopoulos/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Greece is no newcomer to protests. The massive demonstrations that roiled the country at the height of its debt crisis are still remembered vividly by the parents of the Gen Z protesters now out on the streets.
But for the tens of thousands who marched through Athens, Thessaloniki and other cities today, it was France , as well as the perceived shortcomings of a long under-funded education system, that had spurred them into action.
“From Greece to France we’re fighting for public and free education,” proclaimed a giant banner erected above a stage in front of the Athens parliament in Syntagma Square.
Students, school pupils, teachers and university professors take part in a large education protest in Athens, Greece. Photograph: Harris Xanthopoulos/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Singing French partisan songs, Greek students participating in the Athens rally, said the French protests were not only admirable but had been an inspiration.
“ No one is doubting their message or concerns, even if [media] coverage is mostly focused on the violence,” said Fotini, enrolled at a university in the capital.
“We’re here to say we’re with French youth. Our parents endured so many hardships, so much sacrifice, and they feel really upset and enraged that we, too, have so few prospects. A lot of us are still forced to live with our families, even after we graduate, because the cost of living and house rents are so high.”
The protests, which included a one-day ‘solidarity ‘ strike by teachers, have seen students erect tents infront of the Greek parliament to protest against the soaring costs of education.
Many have privately run colleges – a trend that has included British universities establishing branches in the capital – in their sights. “No to private universities. Free and contemporary studies for all,” read another boldly painted banner erected in the plaza.
“No to private universities. Free Contemporary studies for all,” proclaimed a banner erected on Syntagma Square. Photograph: Helena Smith/The Guardian European community affairs correspondent
Much of the news coverage in recent days has focused on the violence that played out on the fringes of the protests in France and Italy.
A woman walks past a building with graffiti that reads "The ultra-rich against everyone" and "No justice, no peace." after the weekend protests over the cost of living turned into rioting and looting across France, in Paris. Photograph: Teresa Suárez/AP The protests themselves, however, point to what seems to be a diverse response to a common crisis: the growing perception, particularly among younger generations, that governments are unable, or unwilling, to deliver when it comes to affordable housing, social equality and robust public services.
“This is the most powerful warning from Europe’s angry youth today, in France and across the continent,” the policy analyst Alberto Alemanno said.
The framing stands in sharp contrast to the many rightwing and far-right voices who have sought to exploit the violence in France and Italy, linking it without evidence to migration while brushing over protesters’ wider demands.
‘A powerful warning’: will Europe’s angry protests lead to real political change?
On Sunday, a mass student movement, Student List, will represent the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power, by putting forward their own candidates in parliamentary elections.
They hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, in a domino effect that could bring a democratic resurgence to central Europe .
Supporters of the Students List stage a protest in front of Serbia's Election Commission headquarters in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/AP Opinion polls have varied wildly, but many expert observers say a close race is quite possible, with neither side prepared to accept a loss as a legitimate result, raising the risk of post-election unrest and clashes.
In order to win, the students’ list of 250 candidates would have to break the mould of Serbian politics, along with Vučić’s grip on the country.
A billboard with an image of Aleksandar Vučić, former authoritarian president, is seen on a closed brewery in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP He stepped down as president last month, five months before the end of his second and last term in office under the constitution, but only with the aim of extending his hold on power as prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).
A student protest movement has gripped Serbia for two years. This weekend it will try to take power
Crowds are also marching in cities across Greece right now calling for better classroom conditions and higher pay for teachers.
Thousands of students, teachers and civil servants have shown up in Athens, with demonstrations also in Thessaloniki and other cities. Some protesters say they’ve been inspired by the rallies in France and Spain.
The primary school teachers union has launched a 24-hour strike while the high school teachers’ federation has also announced a three-hour stoppage, local media report.
Students chant slogans during a protest over rising housing costs and underfunded education, in solidarity with students in France and Spain, in Athens, Greece, October 21, 2026. Photograph: Stelios Misinas/Reuters View image in fullscreen
Nationwide education protests are being held in many cities across Greece, with the participation of school pupils, university students, teachers, and public sector workers. EPA/GEORGE VITSARAS Photograph: George Vitsaras/EPA View image in fullscreen
Students in Athens Photograph: Stelios Misinas/Reuters The Elysée has just announced that the French president Emmanuel Macron has arrived in Saudi Arabia.
As we’ve been reporting, Macron is facing major protests at home, but has embarked on a wider tour of the Gulf, arriving in Qatar yesterday.
His Saudi Arabia stop had not been advertised but it’s not a major surprise – France has recently pledged more military support to the kingdom which is currently fighting the Iran-backed Houthi rebel group in Yemen. France has committed some assistance to protect the state’s oil production facilities.
We are getting a line from Russian news wires that the meeting between Putin and Witkoff has just ended.
US president Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff gestures during his meeting with Russian president Vladimir Putin at the Konstantin Palace in St Petersburg, Russia. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP By the way, this Friday Guardian Europe’s France-based columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in France .
Alexander Hurst and Rokhaya Diallo. Composite: Guardian Design You can send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com , or join the discussion on Friday.
Reader Q&A: What’s next for France after a weekend of riots? Ask our Europe columnists
Meanwhile, two airports have run out of jet fuel, supermarket shelves across southern Italy are standing empty and pharmacies are running short of medicines as lorry drivers continue to blockade roads in protest against soaring fuel prices caused by the war in Iran.
Trucks and passenger vehicles line the roadway during a blockade organized by agricultural workers and truck drivers at the Sant'Onofrio junction in Vibo Valentia, Calabria, Italy. Photograph: Valeria Ferraro/Anadolu/Getty Images Italy’s air traffic management agency, ENAV, said on Wednesday that airports in Crotone and Reggio Calabria had run out of aviation fuel because of disruptions to supplies caused by the protests. It warned that pilots would have to refuel at their departure airports or earlier stops, carrying enough fuel for subsequent flights.
The protests began last week, with lorry drivers blocking roads and slowing traffic across the country, particularly in the south, following strikes and sit-ins by farmers and fishers. The disruption has left supermarket shelves empty in several regions, with photographs showing entire aisles stripped of goods.
Empty shelves are seen inside a supermarket as truck drivers and agricultural workers protest against high living costs and rising fuel prices in Vibo Valentia, Calabria. Photograph: Valeria Ferraro/Anadolu/Getty Images A video of a lorry driver’s teenage daughter breaking down in tears has gone viral after she said her family could no longer afford to go out at weekends because they were struggling to pay their bills.
Italy’s infrastructure minister, Matteo Salvini, has proposed €430m in financial support, but the motorway blockades and lengthy traffic jams continue, putting the government under growing pressure as anger over the cost of living mounts.
The protests have also sparked criticism of Italy’s public broadcaster, Rai, which has been accused of giving greater prominence to violent student demonstrations in Milan than to the economic hardship facing families and lorry drivers in the south. Critics say the coverage plays into the government’s increasingly hardline approach to protests while diverting attention from the growing cost-of-living crisis.

items.title: Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
items.summary: The spire of the clock tower at Limoges city hall dramatically collapsed as it was engulfed in flames on Saturday.
items.content:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.
The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFM TV report.
French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has vowed a "massive" police presence during further protests planned for Saturday, while several cities, including parts of Paris, will be subject to curfews this week.
Marseille mayor BenoÃ®t Payan said on X that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew "starting this evening and for days to come", with French media reporting it would be in place overnight from Tuesday to Friday.
Payan said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.
Paris's police commissioner has also ordered the extension of an overnight curfew in the capital. The PrÃ©fecture de Police said the measure would continue "for as long as it proves necessary".
A curfew for parts of central Lyon was renewed on Tuesday, while overnight curfews for Nice and Lille are ongoing, and a week-long, overnight curfew for Bordeaux came into force on Tuesday night.
French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".
Lecornu told French parliament on Tuesday afternoon a large number of police would meet demonstrators at a planned protest on Saturday.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez previously admitted police had "lost control" in some cities over the weekend.
He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.
Image caption, The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fire
Lecornu also accused far-left groups of an "insurrectionary" plan over the weekend's mass chaos.
Responding to an earlier, similar accusation from Lecornu, left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) de facto leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon had called for the prime minister to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder".
On Tuesday, MÃ©lenchon urged followers on social media to show "restraint" in the face of any "provocation".
Lecornu earlier said targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder.
Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.
Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced on Monday in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
A crowd assembled in Lyon on Monday night in support of businesses affected by the disorder but dispersed without violating the curfew, officials said.
The RhÃ´ne prefecture said on social media that it was "furious" that a far-right group tried to hijack the gathering. The prefecture said on X it reported the group to the public prosecutor for alleged Islamophobic and xenophobic remarks.
Image caption, The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night
Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.
Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.
More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.
Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.
Image caption, Riots took place across French cities, including the capital Paris
More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.
Protest organisers earlier declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.
The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.
Meanwhile, French union La CGT has called for a major day of strikes on 5 November.

items.title: OpenAI to bring AI models to Google's cloud, in further expansion beyond Microsoft
items.summary: OpenAI will now have its models on all three of the top clouds, giving corporate developers more choice.
items.content:
OpenAI bring its AI models to Google's cloud, expands beyond Microsoft
OpenAI said its models will be available for developers through Google's cloud after years of competition between the two companies.
The ChatGPT maker will now have its models on the three major U.S. clouds.
Amazon started hosting OpenAI models in April after exclusivity ended with Microsoft.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman delivers a keynote speech during OpenAI's annual DevDay event in San Francisco, California, US, September 29, 2026.
OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.
For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers. That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.
Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models .
Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.
"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively. All three report quarterly results next week.
Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.
Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when the AI lab said it was using Google's cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface.

The MPSC authorized Consumers Energy to raise its natural gas rates by 4.3% for a typical residential customer on October 15th, allowing the monopoly utility to raise an additional $139.2 million per year from its bill-paying customers, according to Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel.
It is not known at this time what the next rate hike request will be. However, they have announced that the rate hike will be likely filed this December.

In the past, we have asked the MPSC to require both companies to track their costs associated with rate hike cases and, as long as their customers are paying for the process, I hope someday soon we’ll know just how much.”
Consumers Energy sells electricity to approximately 1.9 million customers throughout Michigan and natural gas to 1.8 million customers across the state.

items.title: Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism
items.summary: The Ukrainian leader's hug with Steve Witkoff in the Norwegian capital is unlikely to dispel misgivings about US policy towards his country, writes Paul Adams.
items.content:
Image caption, Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close â that much is obvious â but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, using an expletive while criticising Benjamin Netanyahu's judgement. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.
But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.
The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports â not confirmed by US officials â come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.
Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.
Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Figure caption, Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.
Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.
Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation â again not confirmed by Washington â that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink .
A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink â or its military grade equivalent Starshield â originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.
Image caption, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabated
A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (Â£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.
Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain fromâ¦ digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.
Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

items.title: OpenAI Is Reportedly Raising $30 Billion. Which Chip Stock Gains the Most? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: OpenAI Is Reportedly Raising $30 Billion. Which Chip Stock Gains the Most?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
OpenAI is raising cash again. The ChatGPT maker is seeking around $30 billion in a round that might value it at over $1.4 trillion, Reuters said on Oct. 19. That's up from an $852 billion valuation in March. The talks are still ongoing, though, so nothing's closed.
For chip investors, the bigger number might be what OpenAI has already lined up. In 2025, it announced plans for 26 gigawatts of computing capacity with Nvidia ( NVDA +1.79% ) , Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD +2.88% ) , and Broadcom ( AVGO +0.90% ) . By comparison, OpenAI is reportedly pitching investors on annualized revenue of around $50 billion.
In other words, new cash directly affects whether those plans get paid for. And each of these chip stocks has a different amount riding on it.
Nvidia's September 2025 letter of intent covered at least 10 gigawatts of its systems, and Nvidia planned to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as each gigawatt was deployed.
The backing has since changed form. Nvidia put $30 billion into OpenAI's March round. Then in August, it agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion of obligations at an Ohio data center campus that will house Nvidia hardware under 20-year leases to OpenAI. The first guarantees aren't expected to take effect until fiscal 2029, and Nvidia's exposure drops as OpenAI pays its rent.
A well-funded OpenAI, then, lowers the odds that guarantee ever costs Nvidia anything.
Showing how much is at stake, Nvidia said every generation of its systems at that one site could mean $150 billion to $200 billion in revenue. Yet Nvidia isn't waiting on OpenAI. Its revenue climbed 106% year over year to $96.2 billion in the fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended July 26.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $5.22T
Based on the consensus estimate for fiscal 2028 (the year through January 2028), Nvidia's price-to-earnings ratio is about 14 with shares near $217 as I write. I think that's a modest price for this much growth.
AMD's Oct. 6, 2025, deal covers 6 gigawatts of its graphics processing units (GPUs) , starting with 1 gigawatt in the second half of 2026. Chief financial officer Jean Hu put the expected payoff at "tens of billions of dollars in revenue for AMD."
"We are very happy with our strategic anchor customers in OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic. They are all in the process of ramping," CEO Lisa Su said on AMD's second-quarter earnings call in August.
Meta Platforms signed a matching 6-gigawatt deal, while Anthropic's covers up to 2 gigawatts. That leaves OpenAI with around 43% of the gigawatts across AMD's three anchor customers. And management expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, after second-quarter sales for the segment climbed 107% year over year to $6.7 billion.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $872.95B
The stock already prices much of that in. At roughly $539 as I write, AMD's price-to-earnings ratio on 2027 consensus estimates is near 34 -- more than twice Nvidia's.
Broadcom's 10-gigawatt deal announced Oct. 13, 2025, has OpenAI designing its own artificial intelligence (AI) chips and Broadcom developing and deploying them through 2029.
Broadcom shipped Jalapeño, OpenAI's first custom accelerator, in the quarter ending Aug. 2. On the Sept. 2 earnings call, CEO Hock Tan said Jalapeño is on track for 1.3 gigawatts of deployments in 2027. And he sees OpenAI deploying over 5 gigawatts in 2028, enough to make it Broadcom's second-largest custom-chip customer.
That's when Broadcom's forecast makes its biggest dollar jump. Management expects AI chip revenue to about double to $115 billion in fiscal 2027, then double again to $230 billion in fiscal 2028.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $1.60T
But the money behind OpenAI's deployments is less settled. In June, Broadcom set up a financing vehicle with Apollo Global Management and Blackstone for OpenAI and Anthropic, and the first $35 billion goes to Anthropic's expansion. Asked about financing on the call, Tan mentioned Anthropic's path to an initial public offering .
"OpenAI, we still have less clarity, but it's different," he said.
On analysts' fiscal 2027 estimates, Broadcom's price-to-earnings ratio is around 17 with shares near $335 as of this writing.
Sure, a reported funding round isn't cash in the bank. And $30 billion is small next to OpenAI's chip plans.
Yet if the round closes, I think Broadcom gains the most, because its OpenAI financing is the least settled, and Nvidia arguably gains the least. I'd consider buying all three stocks. But with so much of AMD's plan riding on one customer at over twice Nvidia's price, I'd hold AMD as the smallest position.

Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warn
Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes
The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned.
Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area.
The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting.
The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme.
Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough
Donor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October.
People ride past a pile of burning rubbish in Taiz. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters On Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen.
Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz.
“All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water.
“Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed.
“Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city.
“The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.”
People wait to fill up cooking gas cylinders in Taiz. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters Prices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled.
The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere.
Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers.
The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city.
In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.
UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either the Houthis or the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement.

Comcast Trades at 6 Times Earnings and Yields 6%. Does It Deserve to Be One of the Cheapest S&P 500 Dividend Stocks, or Is This a No-Brainer Buying Opportunity?
Trading at just 6 times forward earnings and with a 6% forward dividend yield, Comcast (NASDAQ: CMCSA) stock is arguably priced for disaster. But is the super-low valuation of this telecommunications and media giant warranted, or have investors overreacted by giving the stock such a "value trap" valuation?
On one hand, there is justification for caution, given the company's ongoing broadband subscriber losses. On the other hand, with Comcast's upcoming plans to spin off the rest of its media assets, it may be on the verge of unlocking its underlying value. Or is it?
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Let's take a closer look to see whether this is a prime deep-value opportunity or a name that's likely to remain a value-and-yield trap.
Image source: Getty Images. Comcast, valuation, and market skepticism
Broadband subscriber losses and their impact on Comcast's profitability remain key drivers of the stock's poor performance and low valuation. Comcast stopped reporting subscriber numbers this year, but as noted in a recent downgrade by KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel, the company is on track to lose 558,000 broadband subscribers in 2026, with another 665,000 expected to "cut the cord" with Comcast in 2027.
Nispel is not alone in his downbeat view on Comcast's dwindling subscriber base. Based on analyst estimates for 2026 and 2027 earnings, it's clear that declining subscribers, and thus declining revenue and earnings for Comcast, remain highly anticipated. Forecasts call for earnings of $3.48 and $3.59 per share in 2026 and 2027, respectively, down from $4.10 per share in 2025.
Still, it's not as if this is the sole factor at play with Comcast shares right now. After last year's spinoff of Versant Media Group (NASDAQ: VSNT), a new entity that owns Comcast's former cable television business, Comcast plans to spin off NBCUniversal and Sky into a separate public company soon.
Analysts anticipate the market rerating these businesses separately, leading to share appreciation, even if earnings aren't set to amaze anytime soon. These bullish price targets range from $31 to $37 per share.
A major reason so many analysts still believe better times lie ahead for the stock price is recent merger activity among telecom stocks and media stocks . Following Charter Communications' purchase of Cox's cable business, there is much speculation that Comcast will merge with Charter, creating new opportunities for cost and growth synergies.
After Skydance (NYSE: SKYD) purchases Warner Bros. Discovery , there's also much speculation that a larger media conglomerate could swallow up NBCUniversal after it becomes independent. However, there are no guarantees. It's unclear whether a Comcast-Charter merger would get through antitrust scrutiny.
After completing such a big transaction, I don't see Skydance rushing in to buy NBCUniversal, either. Other companies could bid for NBCUniversal, but given how peers like Walt Disney already own competing broadcast networks, finding a deep-pocketed buyer may be harder than you think.
In short, consider this catalyst highly speculative. Meanwhile, subscriber losses remain a concern, calling into question the sell side's current view that Comcast's earnings could stabilize in the coming year. Until it can fully shake off this perception, err on the side of caution and avoid the effort to bottom-fish Comcast stock .

Zelenskyy opens door to battle line 'freeze' to end war with Russia
Russia's release of retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard prompts reaction from Zelenskyy during an interview with Brian Kilmeade. The Ukrainian president details negotiations to end the war with Russia, the impact of the Starlink showdown and more during 'Fox & Friends.'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told "Fox & Friends" on Wednesday that he is open to freezing the front lines of the Ukraine-Russia war in an effort to bring the long-running conflict to an end.
Zelenskyy made the remark after being asked by Brian Kilmeade if he would "accept a peace deal that freezes everything the way it is right now, where you still keep 75% or more of your country, regardless of how it started."
"Yes, right now, we have to freeze," Zelenskyy responded. "And I think this is [a] real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire or ‘stop killing’ like President Trump called it.
"Freeze and stop. And, of course, this is the minimum of what we need from Russia today. Then, of course, we will go to [the] president and to Europeans, and we'll ask security guarantees," he continued.
RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks during a press conference on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, in Oslo, Norway. (Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix via AP)
"This is the most important … not to be afraid," Zelenskyy also said. "We need 9.5 million people [who have] lost their houses, which are abroad, everywhere. We need them to come back to Ukraine just to live and to build their country."
Russia has often rejected ceasefire deals with Ukraine, saying they would give Kyiv time to rearm themselves.
VIDEO: TRUMP SUGGESTS ZELENSKYY DOES NOT WANT TO END WAR WITH RUSSIA
Policemen walk in front of destroyed cars in the yard of a multi-story residential building damaged by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka/AP)
"There will be no ceasefire to bring him back to his senses and pump him full of weapons," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week, according to the Interfax news agency.
Zelenskyy said on X Wednesday that "Russia strikes our country virtually every hour."
"Of course, we are not losing this war. But we are losing people. Because of the Russian attacks, we're losing people and time. It's such a pity, because our children don't have a real life and childhood. Not only children, but all people," he wrote in another post.
President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff, left, holds a paper while speaking to Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Konstantin Palace in Strelna, outside St. Petersburg, Russia, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP)
"That's why we need to end this war as quickly as possible. I hope that our partners, Americans and Europeans, will help us. God bless, our strong soldiers stay strong on the battlefield. It helps me stay strong during any kind of negotiations," Zelenskyy added.
The remarks come as President Donald Trump on Wednesday secured the release of Stephen Hubbard from Russia, a retired U.S. teacher who was locked up on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin also agreed Wednesday "in principle" to resume trilateral negotiations with the U.S. and Ukraine after Nov. 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said, according to The Associated Press.
Fox News Digital's Alex Nitzberg contributed to this post.

items.title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
items.summary: Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue AI models.
items.content:
OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring
OpenAI has disclosed two internal coding incidents in which agents weakened the company’s misalignment monitoring safeguards.
Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months.
OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so.
An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks.
"In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech.
The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.
OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.
